def: The differences between individuals in a population, which give selection something to choose between.
The tendency of offspring to resemble their parents because genomes are copied.
The bias by which some individuals leave more offspring than others, so their traits become more common.
The inherited code of an individual, such as DNA in a cell or the source text of a program.
The form a genotype builds and that the world judges, such as an organism's body or a program's behaviour.
The rule that turns a genotype into a phenotype; it decides how much of the variation made by mutation is useful.
A picture in which genotypes are places, neighbours are one mutation apart, and height is fitness.
A genotype fitter than all of its neighbours, where a hill climber that accepts only improvements stops.
Interaction between genes, so that the effect of one depends on the values of others; it makes landscapes rugged.
Kauffman's model in which each of N bits contributes to fitness according to its own value and K other bits.
A change to the genotype that does not change fitness.
Chance changes in which gene variants survive in a finite population, with no help from selection.
A connected set of equally fit genotypes along which a population can wander by neutral mutations.
The capacity of a population or encoding to produce heritable variation that selection can use.
A niching method that divides each individual's score by how many others are nearby, so crowded peaks pay less.
The pattern in which coevolving lineages keep changing without either gaining a lasting advantage.
